Reformed Baptists
ree-FORMD BAP-tists
noun phrase (a confessional tradition)
From “Reformed” (of the Reformed/Calvinistic tradition) and “Baptists”; the confessional tradition holding Reformed doctrine together with believers' baptism, anchored in the 1689 London Baptist Confession.

Biblical Definition

Reformed Baptists are the confessional tradition that holds the doctrines of the Reformed faith—the five solas, the sovereignty of God in salvation, the doctrines of grace—together with the conviction that baptism belongs to believers only, by immersion, as the New Testament pattern. They are the heirs of the Particular Baptists of seventeenth-century England, whose 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith (closely following the Westminster Confession, but differing on baptism, the church, and the civil magistrate) is the dictionary's own primary subordinate standard. The Reformed Baptist holds, with all the Reformed, that God chose His people in Christ before the foundation of the world, that salvation is by grace alone through faith alone, and that He keeps His own to the end. But on baptism he reads the New Testament to teach that the ordinance follows faith: the eunuch was baptized upon confessing that he believed with all his heart; we are buried with Christ by baptism into death, that we should walk in newness of life; he that believeth and is baptized shall be saved. Hence the Reformed Baptist baptizes believers, not infants, and holds the local church to be a gathered company of professing believers. The dictionary, standing in this tradition, marks Reformed Baptists against two misunderstandings: that they are mere Calvinistic versions of revivalist or Arminian Baptists (they are confessional and covenantal, not individualistic), and that their difference from Presbyterians on baptism divides them in the gospel (it does not; they are one with their paedobaptist brethren in the doctrines of grace, differing as friends on the subjects of baptism and church government). The Reformed Baptist tradition is the dictionary's home: Reformed in doctrine, Baptist in the ordinances, confessional in the line of 1689.

Webster 1828 Definition

The confessional tradition holding Reformed doctrine with believers' baptism, anchored in the 1689 London Baptist Confession; the dictionary's own home—Reformed in the doctrines of grace, Baptist in the ordinances, one with paedobaptist brethren in the gospel.

REFORMED BAPTISTS, noun phrase. The tradition holding Reformed doctrine with believers' baptism.

Heirs of the Particular Baptists; anchored in the 1689 London Baptist Confession.

Hold the doctrines of grace and election in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4).

Baptize believers, not infants, upon confession of faith (Acts 8:37; Romans 6:4).

One with paedobaptist Reformed brethren in the gospel, differing on baptism and polity.

Key Scripture

Ac 8:37 — "And Philip said, If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest. And he answered and said, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God."

Ro 6:4 — "Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life."

Mr 16:16 — "He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that believeth not shall be damned."

Eph 1:4 — "According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:"

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the misunderstandings to correct are that Reformed Baptists are mere Calvinistic revivalists, and that their difference from Presbyterians on baptism divides them in the gospel.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two misunderstandings are worth correcting. The first supposes Reformed Baptists to be merely Calvinistic versions of revivalist or Arminian Baptists—individualistic, anti-confessional, suspicious of doctrine. The dictionary, standing in this tradition, answers that Reformed Baptists are confessional and covenantal, anchored in the 1689 London Baptist Confession, holding the whole Reformed system of doctrine: total depravity, unconditional election, definite atonement, effectual calling, and perseverance, with the five solas and the regulative principle of worship. They are not doctrinal minimalists but confessors of a full and historic faith.

The second misunderstanding makes the difference from Presbyterians on baptism a division in the gospel. It is not. Reformed Baptists and paedobaptist Presbyterians and Reformed are one in the doctrines of grace, the five solas, and the sovereignty of God in salvation; they differ as brethren on the subjects of baptism (believers only, by immersion) and on church government (congregational rather than presbyterian). The dictionary holds this difference to be real and worth contending for, yet within the household of faith. The Reformed Baptist tradition is the dictionary's own home—Reformed in doctrine, Baptist in the ordinances, confessional in the line of 1689—and it confesses the same gospel of free and sovereign grace as all the Reformed.

Hebrew Roots

From “Reformed” (the Calvinistic tradition) and “Baptists” (those holding believers' baptism); the heirs of the seventeenth-century Particular Baptists and the 1689 Confession.

expand to see more

“Reformed,” the Calvinistic doctrinal tradition of the doctrines of grace.

“Baptist,” from the conviction of believers' baptism by immersion.

The Particular (as against General/Arminian) Baptists of seventeenth-century England.

The 1689 London Baptist Confession, the tradition's primary subordinate standard.

Distinguished from revivalist and Arminian Baptists by their confessional Calvinism.

Usage

"The teacher described Reformed Baptists as Reformed in doctrine and Baptist in the ordinances."

"He anchored the tradition in the 1689 Confession, against the notion of doctrinal minimalism."

"She held her paedobaptist brethren as one in the gospel, differing only on baptism and polity."
